statement: In people on a stable once-daily methadone dose in an Australian public programme (18 people studied over one 24-hour dosing interval, published 1999), the 9 who reported regular withdrawal before their next dose, compared with the 9 who did not, had a similar methadone level just before the dose (257 against 249 ng/mL) and similar overall exposure, but their level fell faster after the daily peak: fastest fall 74.5 against 47.6 ng/mL per hour, a difference that was not significant in all 18 (P = .09); the paper reports it as significant after 2 people whose urine showed other opioids were left out, but the editors' recalculation gives a two-sided P of about .054. On average, withdrawal symptoms were fewest in the hours after the dose and rose as methadone levels fell, and people whose levels fell fastest reported more withdrawal symptoms (r = 0.60). The groups were formed by self-report, and the study tested no change in treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study of people on methadone, those who felt withdrawal before their next dose had about the same methadone level as others just before the dose, but their level dropped faster after its daily high point. Only 18 people were tested for one day, and the difference was clear only after two people were left out.

statement: In people with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance treatment in high-income countries, periods out of treatment were associated with higher death rates than periods in treatment, with the highest rates in the first four weeks after leaving; three buprenorphine cohorts showed a similar but less certain pattern. A systematic review pooled 19 cohorts published 1974–2016 (18 methadone cohorts, 122,885 people, followed 1965–2010; 3 buprenorphine cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010; 11 in Europe or Israel, 4 in North America, 4 in Australia), counting time in and out of treatment for the same people (Sordo et al., 2017). With methadone, the pooled all-cause death rate was 11.3 per 1,000 person-years in treatment (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2) and 36.1 out of treatment (24.5 to 53.3), an unadjusted difference of 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1) and a ratio of 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86), in 16 cohorts; every cohort had a higher rate out of treatment (cohort rates 5.1 to 39.5 in treatment and 12.4 to 130.2 out). These pooled figures are random-effects averages across very different cohorts (I² 98%): in the three largest, recent register cohorts, which hold 83% of the person-years, the differences were 5.5 to 11.2 and the ratios 1.8 to 2.7, and adding up all deaths and person-years gives 7.1 against 16.4 (editors' calculations from the per-cohort figures). Overdose deaths with methadone (11 cohorts) were 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) in treatment against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4) out, a difference of 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4) and a ratio of 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96), higher out of treatment in every cohort. By time since starting or leaving methadone (five recent cohorts, after the review left out one cohort of people with HIV who inject; one cohort split at two weeks instead of four), the rate was 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) in the first four weeks of treatment against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) for the rest of treatment, a ratio of 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10) that was not statistically significant; and 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) for the rest of the time out of treatment, a difference of 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3) and a ratio of 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74), higher in the first period in each of the five cohorts; the review did not compare the weeks after leaving with time in treatment directly. The rise after leaving was seen in deaths from all causes: in the three methadone cohorts that gave overdose deaths by period, the overdose rate was 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1) later, from 20 overdose deaths in the first period, and in the two cohorts that gave both counts, 18 of the 79 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses (editors' count and calculation); the authors expect overdose deaths to be undercounted and note that deaths from suicide and injury are also more common in that period. With buprenorphine (3 cohorts; 96% of the deaths from Australian studies), the rate was 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) in treatment against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4) out (difference 5.2, −1.0 to 11.4; ratio 2.20, 1.34 to 3.61), 4.5 both in the first four weeks and in the rest of treatment, and 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) in the first four weeks after leaving against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9) later (two cohorts; difference 21.2, −5.9 to 48.2). All pooled estimates are unadjusted; in the cohorts that reported ratios adjusted for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment or illness (five methadone and one buprenorphine cohort for all causes), the ratios were unchanged or larger. But people leave and re-enter treatment for reasons that may themselves affect their risk; the review had no data on why people left or on tolerance or drug use after leaving, and its pooled results do not separate people who finished treatment from people who dropped out or were discharged. Only an appendix table does, for three methadone cohorts, without saying what made treatment 'complete' or 'incomplete': in a nationwide Swedish cohort of 166 people followed 1967–87 and a Tel Aviv cohort of 613 people followed 1993–2008, death rates over the whole time out of treatment were 69.1 against 16.5 per 1,000 person-years after incomplete against complete treatment (26 against 6 deaths; ratio 4.19, 1.72 to 10.18; overdose deaths 58.5 against 13.7, from 22 and 5 deaths) and 83.5 against 25.6 (47 against 5 deaths; ratio 3.26, 1.30 to 8.21), while a UK cohort that counted only the first four weeks after leaving, with methadone and buprenorphine together, found no clear difference (ratio 0.95, 0.24 to 3.73); these comparisons are unadjusted, set different people against each other and rest on few deaths, and the review names the table in its methods without reporting or discussing it. People lost to follow-up may be at higher risk; medicines obtained outside treatment were not captured; and people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or never treated were excluded. The authors suggest that loss of tolerance, assuming many people return to use, and the use of several substances may explain the rise after leaving. The discussion's statement that death rates were significantly lower with buprenorphine than with methadone has no test or estimate in the results. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Is it dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine? The weeks just after leaving treatment were the riskiest time in these studies. In 16 groups of people on methadone in high-income countries, about 11 in 1,000 died each year while in treatment, against about 36 in 1,000 a year after leaving, and every group had more deaths out of treatment; in the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller, about 6 or 7 a year against 12 to 18. In five groups that split time by weeks, deaths in the first 4 weeks after leaving methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on and about 6 after the first month in treatment. The first month on methadone may also carry more risk (about 11 a year per 1,000 people), but that could be chance. Buprenorphine had only three groups, mostly from one Australian study, with fewer deaths in treatment and a rise after leaving, less certainly. The main figures counted everyone who left, for any reason. In an appendix, two small cohorts split people by whether their treatment was classed as complete, without saying what that meant: death rates after leaving were about 3 to 4 times as high after incomplete treatment (about 69 against 17, and 84 against 26, a year per 1,000 people), while a third, which counted only the first 4 weeks after leaving, found no clear difference. The studies could not say why people died: deaths counted as overdoses did not clearly rise after leaving, and nobody recorded tolerance or drug use. People who leave treatment may differ in ways that also affect their risk, so the studies cannot show how much stopping itself raises the risk.
population: People with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance (18 cohorts, 122,885 people, follow-up 1965–2010) or buprenorphine maintenance (3 cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010) in 19 cohorts from high-income countries (11 Europe or Israel, 4 North America, 4 Australia); people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or other treatments, and never-treated people excluded
exposure: Periods out of methadone or buprenorphine maintenance treatment after leaving it, for any reason, with the first four weeks after leaving shown separately; and the first four weeks after starting treatment
comparator: Periods in treatment in the same cohorts (for the interval analyses, the rest of the time in treatment after the first four weeks, and the rest of the time out of treatment after the first four weeks); crude, unadjusted comparisons
outcome: Crude all-cause and overdose death rates per 1,000 person-years, from cohort records and population mortality registers

Buprenorphine, all causes (3 cohorts): 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4); difference 5.2 (−1.0 to 11.4); ratio 2.20 (1.34 to 3.61); by interval (2 cohorts) 4.5 in both treatment periods; first four weeks after leaving 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9), difference 21.2 (−5.9 to 48.2), ratio 2.94 (1.34 to 6.46); overdose (1 cohort) 1.4 against 4.6, and 10.8 against 4.2 out of treatment by interval. statement: As described in a narrative review by the researchers who ran the studies it summarizes (Greenwald et al., 2014, read from the corrected proof), so that every figure here is second-hand, daily buprenorphine under the tongue, compared with placebo, went with fewer of the brain's µ-opioid receptors free to bind a tracer in PET scans, falling as the dose rose, in people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment; responses to heroin and to hydromorphone, another opioid, were reduced but not abolished at the doses studied; and after a daily 16 mg was stopped, the share of free receptors rose over the three days measured. The authors speak of 'availability' (the share of receptors free) rather than 'occupancy', which cannot be measured directly in people; a fall in availability equals a rise in occupancy only if receptor affinity and the body's own opioids stay constant. Scans began 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest time studied, which the authors say probably misses the largest fall. In 3 men given 2 mg, then 16 mg, then placebo, double blind (Zubieta et al., 2000), availability against placebo ranged across brain regions from 50% to 64% at 2 mg a day and from 5% to 21% at 16 mg, and withdrawal and heroin-craving scores fell as the dose rose. In 5 volunteers given 32, 16, 2 and 0 mg a day for 12 days each (Greenwald et al., 2003), the regional means were 53% to 72% at 2 mg, 9% to 20% at 16 mg and 2% to 12% at 32 mg; urine tests showed that they kept using opioids between inpatient stays, even at 32 mg a day. In 7 volunteers taking buprenorphine with naloxone (2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each) and tested 15 hours after the dose, against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005), self-administration of the larger heroin doses offered decreased only modestly at each maintenance dose, when receptor availability, estimated by a model from behaviour rather than imaged, was 21%, 11% and 6%; the authors' re-analysis suggests that nearly all receptors would have to be occupied, beyond what 32 mg a day achieved, to suppress heroin self-administration fully, and in another of their studies 16 mg a day, or 32 mg every other day, did not fully block the reinforcing effect of injected hydromorphone (Greenwald et al., 2002). The review mentions people who try to get past the block with larger amounts of other opioids, but it reports no data on what happens when they do. In 10 volunteers stabilized on 16 mg a day and then switched, double blind, to placebo (Greenwald et al., 2007), scans 4, 28, 52 and 76 hours after the last dose gave availability of 27% to 31%, 54% to 61%, 65% to 75% and 77% to 94%, against the placebo condition of the 2003 study (other people); after the authors adjusted the 4-hour values to the 2003 study, their fitted curves give 13% to 25% at 4 hours, 37% to 46% at 24 hours, 56% to 73% at 48 hours and 75% to 90% at 72 hours (values between scans are read from the curves, and the adjusted 4-hour range does not match the 2003 study's 9% to 20%). In the same study, the subjective effects of injected hydromorphone were significantly smaller at 4 and 28 hours than at 52 and 76 hours, a recovery the authors call modest. The review's abstract states as results that suppressing withdrawal appears to need 50% availability or less, and that blocking the reinforcing and subjective effects of typical doses of other opioids needs less than 20% (less than 10% against higher-than-usual doses); but its body says that there is no agreed definition of a block and that the availability needed for either effect is not known, its summary says that blockade 'has not been reliably observed under BUP dosing conditions studied to date', and the 20% figure comes from preliminary modelling. The volunteers were relatively healthy, mostly men, aged 18 to 50, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine, and dependent on heroin; the authors call it unclear whether the findings apply to people seeking treatment or dependent on other opioids; fentanyl was not studied; the scans used buprenorphine without naloxone, although the authors cite data that products under the tongue with and without naloxone have similar effects; and the review reports no results on breathing or overdose, so it says nothing about the risk of overdose when other opioids are used on or after buprenorphine. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: Does Suboxone block other opioids, and for how long? Only partly, in the small laboratory studies summarized in one review by the researchers who ran them. In brain scans of people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment, buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) took up more of the brain's opioid receptors the higher the daily dose: at 16 mg a day, only about 9 to 20 in 100 receptors were still free 4 hours after the dose. Even so, heroin and another opioid, hydromorphone, still had some effect at the highest doses tested, and the volunteers kept using opioids between their hospital stays. The review mentions people who take larger amounts of other opioids to get past the block, but it has no data on what happens when they do. After 10 volunteers stopped 16 mg a day, the share of free receptors rose steadily over the 3 days of scans, from about 13 to 25 in 100 at 4 hours to about 75 to 90 in 100 at 3 days, and an injected opioid was blunted more at 4 and 28 hours than at 52 and 76 hours. The review's summary names receptor levels needed to block other opioids, but its authors say nobody knows them and that a full block was never reliably seen. The studies had 3 to 10 people each, mostly men, all dependent on heroin; fentanyl was not studied, and the review reports nothing on breathing or overdose.
population: People dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment, studied as inpatients in laboratory studies by the review's authors, as described in one narrative review: 3 men (Zubieta et al., 2000), 5 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2003), 10 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2007; 5 heavier and 5 lighter smokers) and 7 volunteers on buprenorphine with naloxone against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); in the scan studies aged 18 to 50, many fewer women than men, relatively healthy, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine

statement: In people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl and who had taken buprenorphine after fentanyl, remembering severe withdrawal on taking it was common, and more common the shorter the shortest wait after fentanyl that people reported, in one self-report survey analysed without adjustment (Varshneya et al., 2022, read from the author manuscript). Of 1,679 people whose answers were collected at admission by an outcomes-tracking system, 1,163 (69.3%) reported fentanyl use; 421 of them had never taken buprenorphine after fentanyl and 57 had done so only with a shortest wait of 1 month to 1 year. Of the 685 whose shortest wait was under 1 month, 250 (36.5%; 95% CI 33.0 to 40.2, editors' calculation) said their withdrawal symptoms on taking buprenorphine after fentanyl had been severe, 136 (19.9%) moderate, 122 (17.8%) mild and 177 (25.8%) none; of 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl, 30 (15.0%) said severe. Severe withdrawal after buprenorphine was remembered by 152 of the 339 people whose shortest wait was under 24 hours (44.8%) and 55 of the 160 whose shortest wait was 24 to 48 hours (34.4%), and, by the editors' reconstruction from the printed odds ratios (checked against the bars of Figure 1), by 25 of 97 at 48 to 72 hours (25.8%), 13 of 52 at 72 hours to 1 week (25.0%) and 5 of 37 at 1 week to 1 month (13.5%): a gradual fall, with no clear cut-off. The abstract's 22.19% for 'those who waited less than 24 hours' is 152 out of all 685, not out of the 339 who waited less than 24 hours (editors' calculation). The paper's odds ratios for severe withdrawal (under 24 hours 5.20, 95% CI 1.98 to 13.68; 24 to 48 hours 3.35, 1.24 to 9.09; 48 to 72 hours 2.22, 0.78 to 6.33; 72 hours to 1 week 2.13, 0.69 to 6.62) are unadjusted and compare each group with a reference the paper does not name, which the editors' exact reproduction shows to be the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month; the results call the odds ratios of about 2 at 48 hours to 1 week no increase, and the conclusion compares with everyone who waited more than 48 hours, which the model did not do. The answers were remembered when people entered treatment, about one or more unspecified occasions; the shortest wait ever was not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal; the survey did not record the dose, form, setting or supervision of the buprenorphine, or whether withdrawal had begun before it was taken; and a single rating cannot tell withdrawal that buprenorphine brought on from withdrawal it did not relieve (the authors explain severe withdrawal after methadone as too little opioid effect early in treatment). The survey period, response rate, full questionnaire and centres are not described, and the descriptive appendix was not on file. Among the 152 people who had taken both medicines after fentanyl, 69 (45.4%) remembered severe withdrawal after buprenorphine and 20 (13.2%) after methadone. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Can Suboxone put you in withdrawal if you use fentanyl? Many people say it did. In a survey of people starting treatment at 49 US centres who said they used fentanyl, 250 of 685 who had taken buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal when they took it, 37 in 100, against 15 in 100 of those who had taken methadone after fentanyl. The shorter the shortest wait after fentanyl that people reported, the more often they remembered severe withdrawal: about 45 in 100 when it was under a day, 34 in 100 at one to two days, about 25 in 100 at two days to a week and 14 in 100 at a week to a month, with no clear cut-off. These are memories collected when people started treatment, about occasions nobody recorded. The survey did not know the dose, the form or who gave it, it allowed for nothing else that differed between people, and one question cannot tell withdrawal that buprenorphine brought on from withdrawal it failed to relieve. The paper's own summary gives 22 in 100 for those who waited under a day, but that is out of all 685 people, not out of the 339 who waited that little.
population: People entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres using one outcomes-tracking system (survey period and centres not described) whose main drug was opioids and who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl before treatment: 1,163 of 1,679 (mean age 30.8 years; 70.6% men; 80.4% White; 43.9% said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission); withdrawal ratings analysed for the 685 whose shortest wait after fentanyl before buprenorphine was under 1 month and for 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl
exposure: Taking buprenorphine after fentanyl (any product; the table note names seven brands, Suboxone among them), grouped by the shortest time people said they had ever waited after fentanyl: under 24 hours, 24 to 48 hours, 48 to 72 hours, 72 hours to 1 week, 1 week to 1 month; dose, form, setting and supervision not recorded

magnitude: Varshneya et al. (2022), Table 1 and text. Fentanyl use reported by 1,163 of 1,679 (69.3%; probably 180, definitely 983). In the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims of 2013–2017, 8,996 people met these conditions (61.0% women, 91.5% White, 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day). Stopping meant a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out, and the 6 months were counted from the last day of supply. In those 6 months, 464 people (5.2%; 95% CI 4.7 to 5.6, editors' calculation) had at least one medically treated overdose, opioid or non-opioid (5.1% to 5.5% in the four groups by length of treatment; 5.6% among the 8,077 with a recorded diagnosis of opioid use disorder); 41.2% to 48.6% had at least one emergency department visit, 11.3% to 13.9% at least one hospital admission, and 19.1% to 25.9% filled a prescription for a full-agonist opioid, which the authors read as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care. Against people treated for 6 to 9 months (4,126), those treated for 15 to 18 months (931) had lower adjusted odds of emergency visits (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.86), hospital admission (0.79, 0.64 to 0.99) and opioid prescriptions (0.67, 0.56 to 0.80), and those treated for 12 to 15 months lower odds of emergency visits (0.84) and opioid prescriptions (0.84), but the odds of overdose did not differ (15 to 18 months 1.04, 0.75 to 1.44, an interval that allows odds about 25% lower to 44% higher, editors' reading). Overdose after stopping was more likely with a recorded psychiatric diagnosis (odds ratio 1.61), alcohol use disorder (2.02) or another drug use disorder (1.51), and less likely in women (0.65). Because no group continued buprenorphine, the study cannot say whether stopping raised these risks compared with staying on treatment; the records do not say why anyone stopped; and the comparison of durations is adjusted only for age, sex, race, plan type, recorded diagnoses and starting dose, which the authors say leaves residual confounding possible. Deaths are not recorded: anyone who died, or lost Medicaid for any other reason, in the 6 months after stopping was excluded (3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped within the study window, 30.5%, editors' calculation), so fatal overdoses are not counted, as the authors say, and the figures are not the full risk after stopping. Only overdoses billed to Medicaid were counted, and the code list is printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50, which leaves out T40.0 to T40.4, the codes for poisoning by opium, heroin, methadone and other opioids (study card note), although the same sentence says that opioid overdoses were counted; the codes used are in an online table (S1) that was not on file. The people studied had all stayed in treatment at least 6 months, a minority the authors describe as likely relatively stable, so the figures may not apply to people who stop in the first weeks or months, or outside Medicaid. The discussion's statement that overdose rates after stopping are two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder gives no figures and sets this study's medically treated overdoses beside death rates from another study, so it is not used here. Death rates during and after methadone or buprenorphine treatment, from a review of cohort studies, are a separate answer (see the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: What happens after stopping Suboxone? In US Medicaid records of 8,996 people who stopped buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) after 6 to 18 months of treatment, about 5 in 100 had at least one overdose treated by a doctor or hospital in the next 6 months. In those 6 months, 41 to 49 in 100 went to an emergency department, 11 to 14 in 100 stayed in hospital, and 19 to 26 in 100 filled a prescription for another opioid. People who had been on buprenorphine for 15 to 18 months had fewer emergency visits, hospital stays and opioid prescriptions afterwards than people who stopped after 6 to 9 months, but no fewer overdoses. Nobody in the study stayed on treatment, so it cannot say whether stopping raised the risk, and the records do not say why people stopped. People who died, or lost their Medicaid cover, in those 6 months were left out, so overdoses that killed people are not counted. Deaths during and after treatment are covered in a separate answer.
population: Adults aged 18 to 64 in the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims database (2013–2017; contributing states not named) who began a new buprenorphine episode for opioid use disorder, stayed on it continuously for 6 to 18 months, then stopped, and stayed enrolled in Medicaid for the 6 months afterwards: 8,996 people (61.0% women; 91.5% White; 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day); people also covered by Medicare were excluded
exposure: Stopping buprenorphine (a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out) after 6–9 (4,126 people), 9–12 (2,440), 12–15 (1,499) or 15–18 months (931) of continuous treatment, by days supplied in pharmacy claims; the 6 months of follow-up counted from the last day of supply
comparator: No group that continued buprenorphine. The longer-treatment groups against the 6–9-month group, adjusted for age, sex, race (White or not), Medicaid plan type, recorded psychiatric, alcohol and other drug use disorder diagnoses, and starting dose
outcome: At least one medically treated drug overdose, opioid or non-opioid (ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50), at least one emergency department visit, at least one inpatient admission, and at least one filled full-agonist opioid prescription, in Medicaid claims in the 6 months after stopping; deaths not recorded
magnitude: Williams et al. (2020). Flow: 26,576 with a new continuous episode of more than 6 months; 10,481 who did not stop (39.4%, editors) and 3,159 who stopped too late in the study window removed; 12,936 who stopped within the window; 3,940 (30.5%, editors) removed for incomplete enrolment in the 6 months after stopping; 8,996 analysed (6–9 months 4,126; 9–12 months 2,440; 12–15 months 1,499; 15–18 months 931). Six-month outcomes across the four groups, unadjusted: emergency department visit 41.2–48.6% (abstract 42.1–49.9%), inpatient admission 11.3–13.9%, full-agonist opioid prescription 19.1–25.9%, medically treated overdose 5.1–5.5%; overall overdose 464/8,996 = 5.2% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–5.6, editors). 15–18 against 6–9 months, unadjusted: emergency visits 41.2% against 48.6% (p < 0.001), admissions 11.3% against 13.9% (p < 0.05), opioid prescriptions 19.1% against 25.9% (p < 0.001). Adjusted odds ratios against 6–9 months (Table 2): 15–18 months, admission 0.79 (0.64–0.99), emergency visit 0.75 (0.65–0.86), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44), opioid prescription 0.67 (0.56–0.80); 12–15 months 0.86 (0.72–1.03), 0.84 (0.75–0.95), 1.10 (0.84–1.43), 0.84 (0.73–0.97); 9–12 months 0.86 (0.74–1.01), 0.94 (0.85–1.04), 1.04 (0.82–1.30), 0.95 (0.85–1.07). Overdose, other terms in the same model: women 0.65 (0.54–0.79); psychiatric diagnosis 1.61 (1.32–1.96); alcohol use disorder 2.02 (1.47–2.79); non-opioid drug use disorder 1.51 (1.22–1.86); starting dose 1.00 per mg (0.97–1.04). Sensitivity analysis (8,077 with a recorded opioid use disorder diagnosis): 15–18 against 6–9 months, emergency visits 0.74 (0.64–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.63–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.68 (0.56–0.82); odds of overdose equivalent across groups, 5.6% overall.

risk_of_bias.note: Coverage and measurement could change the figures materially (card sc_williams_2020, ROBINS-I serious): 3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped (30.5%) were excluded for losing Medicaid in the 6 months after stopping, a group that includes everyone who died; overdoses count only if billed to Medicaid; the printed code list leaves out the opioid codes, and the table of the codes used was not read.

inconsistency.note: One study; the four duration groups give similar overdose rates (5.1% to 5.5%).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Medicaid enrollees who stopped after at least 6 months and stayed enrolled; the statement says the figures leave out deaths, may not apply to people who stop early or are outside Medicaid, and come with no group that stayed on treatment.

imprecision.note: 464 overdoses; the overall share has a narrow interval (4.7% to 5.6%). The duration comparison for overdose is imprecise (0.75 to 1.44) and is worded as no detected difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all four outcomes are reported for every comparison, including the null overdose result.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (how many people had each event in the 6 months after stopping): starts low; down one level for risk of bias, because exclusions that include every death and an overdose definition that cannot be checked could change the figures materially: very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. The comparisons by length of treatment are associations in the same records, open to confounding by why and when people stopped, and are not rated separately; the authors concede the design cannot show cause. Nothing here compares stopping with continuing: deaths during and after treatment are the subject of the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine, which rests on a review of cohort studies and measures deaths, not treated overdoses; the two do not conflict. Status: single study.
